tldr: We propose a self-supervised learning framework that extracts a physical footstep instability score from factor graph residuals in legged state estimation, projects it onto forward-facing camera images, and trains a visual predictor to anticipate and avoid hazardous footholds based on visual appearance.
hero_caption: Offline self-supervised label generation pipeline. Stance phases are extracted from contact detection, and contact constraint residuals from a factor graph are aggregated into per-footstep instability scores. These are back-projected into past camera images via external odometry to form sparse supervisory label masks.
overview:
For quadrupedal robots navigating natural, unstructured terrain, deciding where to step is critical for survival. Hidden tree roots under fallen leaves, mud, and slippery slopes cannot be judged as safe or unsafe from 3D geometry alone. Robots require human-like visual anticipation of ground yield before committing to a step. However, using self-supervised learning for this has been hindered by the fundamental challenge of defining what constitutes an 'unstable contact' supervisory signal.

The authors addressed this by looking into a classical robotics tool: legged state estimation. Legged odometry typically assumes a rigid contact model where a foot on the ground remains stationary without slipping. When a foot slips or sinks, this assumption breaks, causing the factor graph optimization residual—the mismatch between prediction and measurement—to spike. TACOS (Terrain-Aware COntact Supervision) reuses this residual directly as a physically grounded, meaningful metric of footstep instability.

The authors formulate two variants: an offline 'hard score' that uses the full optimization window with hindsight, and a causally computed 'soft score' available immediately. These scores are projected onto preceding camera images to train a dense visual instability predictor (DPT) from sparse foothold footprints.

Evaluated on 1,716 manually annotated contacts, TACOS outperformed existing force- and kinematics-based approaches, improving the Volume Under the Surface (VUS) for severity ranking by 28%. It also improved visual rank correlation by 58% on unseen outdoor test runs. Finally, in a closed-loop autonomous walking experiment across a 50 m forest trajectory, the real robot skillfully avoided sinking into mud and colliding with fallen branches.
contributions: Formulated novel self-supervised footstep instability scores (an accurate hindsight-based hard score and an immediate causal soft score) derived from contact constraint residuals in legged odometry factor graphs.

Demonstrated on both a human-annotated contact dataset and unseen outdoor walking runs that the proposed scores significantly outperform existing alternatives in detecting contact hazards and supervising visual predictors.

Showed that conditioning the visual predictor on onboard context, such as camera tilt and recent footstep history, further enhances predictive accuracy, validating its efficacy in closed-loop footstep planning on a real robot in a forest.

sections.heading: Looks Can Be Deceiving: Why Walking in Nature Requires Visual Anticipation
sections.summary: In unstructured environments like forests, terrains that appear geometrically flat can still be slippery or soft, causing purely geometry-based footstep planners to fail. This paper presents TACOS, a framework that leverages contact model residuals from state estimation to learn footstep instability in a self-supervised manner and anticipate hazards visually.
sections.details:
Quadrupedal robots hold great promise for demanding missions such as search and rescue or environmental monitoring. However, selecting reliable footholds on natural rough terrain remains a critical challenge. As seen in Figure F1, tree roots hidden beneath benign-looking leaf litter can trap feet, and slick mud can cause severe falls. Crucial physical properties like compliance and friction cannot be deduced from 3D geometric shapes alone.

When humans walk, our visual system subconsciously predicts how the ground will yield before taking a step. Researchers have explored reinforcement learning and self-supervised learning to give robots this capability. However, reinforcement learning directly from high-dimensional camera images suffers from poor sample efficiency, while self-supervised methods struggle with how to define an instability supervisory signal. Relying on robot-wide tracking errors or power draw yields only whole-body feedback, lacking per-leg spatial resolution to identify which foot slipped. Conversely, instrumenting feet with force sensors is often impractical due to hardware fragility and high costs.

To solve this, the authors turned to the underlying mathematics of legged odometry. State estimators assume that stance feet remain stationary on the ground. When a foot slips or sinks, that assumption breaks, manifesting as an optimization residual in the factor graph. TACOS aggregates these residuals into per-footstep instability scores and projects them onto camera images to train a dense visual predictor.

captions.F1: A quadrupedal robot traversing a forest environment. In rough terrain littered with roots and leaves, geometry alone cannot determine safety; hidden roots can trap a foot and lead to a fall (bottom-right white box), as shown in the GoPro view.

sections.heading: Turning State Estimation 'Trash' into Visual Learning 'Treasure'
sections.summary: Previous works treated contact inconsistencies in legged state estimation merely as noise to discard or downweight for reactive odometry correction. This work reframes those violations as direct physical measurements of foot-ground interaction, elevating them into supervisory signals for proactive visual foresight.
sections.details:
### II-A Legged State Estimation
In legged robot state estimation, the kinematic constraint that stance feet are stationary relative to the ground is used to arrest IMU drift. When a foot slips or the ground yields, kinematics and inertial data disagree. Conventional contact-aware estimators (such as Invariant Smoothers) detect these inconsistent contacts reactively to exclude or downweight them in odometry optimization. TACOS recognizes that this discarded inconsistency is actually a direct physical measurement of terrain hazard.

### II-B Estimating Footstep Instability
Prior efforts to quantify footstep instability fall broadly into force-based and kinematics-based methods. Approaches using force sensors (e.g., GRS) or joint torque estimators can be sensitive to joint friction and drivetrain backlash, and foot-mounted force sensors are rarely present on commercial quadrupeds. Conversely, kinematics-based slip detection methods (such as OCELOT or sliding metrics) analyze foot displacement or relative velocity to swing legs. However, most classify slip as a binary event rather than capturing the continuous severity of instability.

### II-C Self-Supervised Terrain Learning
Prior self-supervised terrain learning frameworks rely on vehicle-level metrics like velocity tracking error (WVN), actuator current (P-STEER), or human teleoperation preferences. However, these lack per-foot spatial resolution. Furthermore, because a robot traverses only a small fraction of the visual scene, many prior methods aggressively densify labels across the image using semantic segmentation. In heterogeneous natural environments, adjacent patches that look visually similar often possess vastly different physical properties. TACOS avoids pseudo-label densification, supervising only the sparse footprint regions with actual physical contact.

sections.heading: From Factor Graph Residuals to Dense Visual Predictors: The TACOS Pipeline
sections.summary: The authors construct an end-to-end pipeline: isolating stance phases, aggregating factor graph residuals into instability scores, back-projecting them into images, and training a DPT-based dense visual predictor. Two score formulations are provided: an offline hard score with hindsight, and an immediate causal soft score.
sections.details:
### III-A Contact Detection and Stance Refinement
Computing accurate scores requires precisely identifying the stance phase $\mathcal{S}_i$ when the foot is on the ground. Raw contact signals on robots like ANYmal can be noisy, so morphological operations are applied: contacts shorter than 100 ms are removed, and gaps under 25 ms are bridged. Furthermore, to prevent lift-off dynamics from triggering false instability, the stance is terminated at the last point where vertical ground reaction force (GRF) exceeds 50 N within 150 ms of lift-off.

### III-B Residual-Based Instability Formulations
Within a fixed-lag factor graph, residuals $\mathbf{d}_{i,k}$ between forward kinematics of the stance foot and the world-frame foothold position $\mathbf{f}_{i,k}$ are evaluated. Residuals are normalized by an empirical contact covariance $\sigma_{\mathrm{ct}} = 8\text{ cm}$.
- **Hard Score ($m_{i,\mathrm{hard}}$)**: Assumes the foothold remains completely stationary throughout the stance (sharing a single $\mathbf{f}_i$). The score is computed as the maximum normalized residual across the stance phase after leaving the smoother window. This serves as the reference benchmark.
- **Soft Score ($m_{i,\mathrm{soft}}$)**: Allows the foothold position to drift slightly via a small random walk ($\sigma_{\mathrm{rw}}^2 = 0.04\text{ m}^2/\text{s}$). The residual can be evaluated causally in real time immediately after each update, aggregated via the 95th percentile.

### III-C Image Association and Projection
Foothold locations are projected into past camera images using poses from an external LiDAR-inertial odometry system (FAST-LIVO2), which remains unaffected by foot slip. Footholds recorded within the past 10 seconds and between 0.5 to 3 m in front of the camera are rasterized as 6 cm diameter foot-sized circles.

### III-D Visual Instability Predictor
The architecture employs a frozen DINOv3-Base encoder paired with a Dense Prediction Transformer (DPT) decoder (Figure F3). Robot orientation (roll and pitch) and recent average footstep instability for the front and rear feet are embedded into context tokens and fused across decoder stages via Gated Cross-Attention (GCA). The network is trained with a masked Huber loss computed solely over the sparse footprint pixels.

### III-E Footstep Planning
The predicted dense instability map is projected onto a local ground plane fitted to the four stance feet, populating a 5 m $\times$ 5 m costmap (4 cm resolution). During each swing phase, a contact-tracking policy chooses the safest foothold within 25 cm of the nominal step target via minimum-cost optimization.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: From Benchmark Evaluations to Closed-Loop Forest Traversal
sections.summary: Across 1,716 manually annotated contacts, TACOS outperformed existing alternatives by 28% in severity ranking (VUS). In visual prediction on unseen outdoor environments, it improved Spearman rank correlation by 58%. Closed-loop trials in a forest demonstrated successful avoidance of mud pits and fallen branches.
sections.details:
### IV-A Validation of Instability Scores
ANYmal-D was operated across three challenging terrains: an ice rink, a log pile, and a slippery 45-degree slope. Human annotators labeled 1,716 contact events (275 unstable) from foot-facing GoPro footage, assigning severity levels (Low, Medium, High).
In contact detection Average Precision (AP), the hard score achieved 0.96 and the soft score achieved 0.93, compared to 0.90 for the best baseline. For Volume Under the Surface (VUS)—evaluating multiclass ranking across severity tiers—the hard score achieved 0.893 versus 0.700 for the strongest alternative, an improvement of 28% (Figure F5). Hard scores excelled at detecting sustained slips on ice, whereas soft scores were particularly sensitive to abrupt slips on logs, highlighting their complementary qualities.

### IV-B Visual Instability Prediction Evaluation
Visual prediction was evaluated on three unseen outdoor runs from the large-scale GrandTour dataset. As shown qualitatively in Figure F6, WVN's whole-body supervision yields coarse maps, and force-sensor PCA (GRS) produces blurred boundaries. In contrast, hard TACOS cleanly separates railway ties from surrounding ballast and forest trails from bordering vegetation.
Quantitatively, hard TACOS achieved a median Spearman rank correlation of $\rho = 0.554$, outperforming baselines by 58%. An ablation study on onboard context (Table II) showed that conditioning on recent footstep history boosted correlation by an additional 25%, proving the model effectively leverages the continuity of terrain physical properties.

### IV-C Closed-Loop Field Experiment in a Forest
The trained predictor ran onboard an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor at 10 Hz over a 50 m forest trail (Figure F8). Baseline geometry-only (elevation map) navigation failed: it stepped deeply into a benign-looking mud pit (Point A) and got stuck mistaking traversable tall grass (Point B) for an impassable obstacle. In contrast, the TACOS-guided planner correctly identified the mud as hazardous, navigated through the tall grass, and stepped over a fallen branch (Point C) onto stable ground.

captions.F6: Predicted costmaps on unseen outdoor scenes. Top: input image; middle: WVN and GRS; bottom: Hard TACOS. TACOS resolves railway ties from gravel and trails from surrounding brush with high spatial precision.
captions.F8: Closed-loop 50 m forest traversal comparison. Geometry-only planning (middle) sinks into a mud pit (A) and halts at tall grass (B). TACOS (right) navigates the entire trail by evading mud, stepping through grass, and avoiding fallen branches (C).

sections.heading: Conclusion and What's Next
sections.summary: TACOS demonstrates that treating factor graph residuals from legged state estimation as self-supervision enables accurate visual anticipation and avoidance of hazardous footholds. Future avenues include integrating depth sensing and implementing continual online learning.
sections.details:
TACOS introduces an elegant, highly effective concept: reinterpreting contact constraint violations (residuals) in legged odometry directly as supervisory signals for footstep instability. Both the hindsight-enabled hard score and the causal soft score substantially outperform existing metrics in human benchmark comparisons and visual model training.

However, label quality still relies on accurate stance detection, drift-free state estimation, and precise camera-to-kinematics time synchronization. The authors note that future work will explore fusing RGB imagery with depth and geometric representations, as well as enabling continual learning so quadrupeds can adapt their visual models online as they encounter novel terrains.

takeaways: Turning state estimation inconsistencies (optimization residuals) on their head provides an exceptionally powerful, self-supervised metric for physical footstep hazards.
Supervising dense visual models strictly on sparse, physically grounded footprint labels yields sharper terrain boundaries than artificially densifying labels across entire image patches.
Conditioning visual footstep predictors on onboard context, such as body posture and recent footstep instability history, dramatically enhances predictive accuracy.
limitations: Relies heavily on accurate stance segmentation and drift-free external odometry (such as LiDAR-inertial SLAM); tracking errors or misidentified contacts directly introduce label noise.

Currently maps predictions to 3D local costmaps using a local ground plane approximation from RGB imagery, which may introduce projection errors on rugged terrains with steep ledges or complex vertical structures.
Operates with a frozen, pre-trained model and does not yet support continual online adaptation when encountering completely novel soil or surface types.
